name: MN3007
description: 1024-stage bucket-brigade delay line, the shorter-delay half-sibling of the MN3005. Variable analog delay of 5.12-51.2ms depending on clock frequency (10-100kHz). The workhorse chorus/flanger BBD, used in classics like the Boss CE-1 and Electro-Harmonix Clone Theory. Needs an external clock generator (commonly an MN3101-style companion clock-driver chip) to drive CP1/CP2.

pins.name: VCC
pins.description: positive supply (a few volts above VDD, see datasheet bias network)

pins.name: VDD
pins.description: negative supply (typically -15V referenced to GND in the classic bias scheme)

DIP-8.notes: Per Panasonic's own block diagram/pinout, DIP-8, top view. OUT1/OUT2 are two clock-phase-interleaved outputs of the same delay line, typically summed externally.

extra.supply: VDD=-15V, VGG=VDD+1 (per Panasonic's bias scheme; see application notes for the exact bias network)

typical_application: Analog chorus, flanger, and short-slapback delay/reverb effects in guitar pedals and electronic musical instruments. Requires an external clock (e.g. an MN3101-class clock driver) and a low-pass anti-aliasing filter on the output to remove residual clock feedthrough.
gotchas: needs an external clock generator driving CP1/CP2 with complementary, non-overlapping phases; it is not self-clocking
delay time is inversely proportional to clock frequency: higher clock = shorter delay, lower clock = longer delay (and worse bandwidth/noise)
clock feedthrough onto the output is normal and expected; always follow with a low-pass filter tuned below the clock frequency
bias supply scheme (VDD/VGG relationship) matters for headroom and noise; follow a proven reference circuit (e.g. the classic Panasonic application notes) rather than guessing bias values
genuine NOS Panasonic/Matsushita chips are increasingly scarce; some modern builds substitute other MN3xxx-family or clone BBD chips with similar but not identical specs
